articles.title: 'Treason': Trump accused of 'incredible level of corruption' after Nvidia reversal
articles.description: National security veterans and researchers were floored by the "level of corruption" displayed by Nvidia and President Donald Trump after the chipmaker cited his administration's input in reinstating its CEO. Nvidia's board voted unanimously on Monday to bring Jensen Huang back as president and chief executive, saying it was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese asset, The New York Times reported. "In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," the board said. The board did not say which officials gave that input, and critics seized on the gap. "No national security risk?" Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) wrote on X. "Based on what?" "The board needs to be asked WHO at the senior level of the U.S. government assured them Huang wasn't a security risk," Bulwark editor-at-large Bill Kristol wrote on X. "This is nuts," Reuters national security correspondent Erin Banco posted. "You can't just wave a magic wand and declare 'there's no national security risk'. We're not in The Office." Others said the administration had put the stock market ahead of national security. "So the Trump administration told Nvidia to overlook the national security threat and reinstate Huang because they like what the market looks like when he's leading the company," behavioral scientist Caroline Orr Bueno, who studies disinformation, wrote on X. "Just an incredible level of corruption." "The President is selling out our national security to keep the stock market high and probably for some f— donation to his ballroom," Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) wrote. Nvidia has already given to Trump's White House ballroom. Its $25 million gift tied Apple's for the largest on a confidential list of donors, The Washington Post reported in October. Some critics went further, accusing Trump of working for China. "Trump now works on behalf of China, as well as Russia," former CIA officer John Sipher wrote on Bluesky. "Trump got his wish here," former National Security Agency analyst John Schindler wrote. "Which is also Beijing's wish. Odd, no?" "Don't get this wrong: it's not that he cares more about the stock market than national security," disinformation researcher Dave Troy wrote. "It's that he cares more about Chinese security than American security. The treason is always paramount." Nvidia said it had received assurances from Trump's administration after the president publicly pushed for Huang's return. "I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday evening. On Monday morning, Trump signaled Huang was already back in the job before Nvidia posted the news. "He's back where he should be and we see he did absolutely nothing wrong from that standpoint," Trump told PBS News Hour White House correspondent Liz Landers after declining to discuss reporting that the woman had been in touch with an official of China's top spy agency. "Yep, well, he will be soon hopefully," Trump said when Landers asked whether he meant Huang. Landers posted the exchange at 8:29 a.m., and Nvidia's newsroom account posted the announcement on X at 8:58 a.m. "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security," Trump wrote on Truth Social after the announcement. He added that the attorney general had confirmed the government "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." Nvidia said a committee of independent directors will see its investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort through to completion.

articles.title: Robot submarine exploring world's deepest ocean trench finds unprecedented volcanic activity
articles.description: Fifty-two million years ago, the Pacific tectonic plate began to slide under the Philippine Sea plate, forming the Mariana Trench, the deepest known valley on the Earth's ocean floor. The deepest part of this abyss, the Challenger Deep, is almost 11,000 meters (36,000 feet) below sea level. But why is it so deep? Scientists trying to answer this question sent a remotely operated vehicle to collect samples around the Deep, where they found evidence of the world's deepest underwater explosive volcanic eruptions.

articles.title: Godzilla Minus Zero: A review
articles.description: Three years after Godzilla Minus One splashed onto the scene with a new, terrifying Godzilla and a riveting narrative, director Takashi Yamazaki brings everyone's favorite monster back to the big screen in Godzilla Minus Zero. The shrill, fervent cry of violins pierces the tense atmosphere as the kaijus arrive in all their glory, tearing through villages and cities easily as if they were made of Legos. Within the first five minutes, the viewer is plunged into the chaos, meeting characters old and new, and reckoning with new threats that place Godzilla in a whole new light. A wild Ghidorah appears Godzilla takes his time to shine. While you wait, meet Ghidorah: a giant yellow dragon that fires electricity from his mouth as he terrorizes a small city. He is an alien who takes on the properties of those he kills, and he is made a king when the protagonists of Godzilla Minus Zero try to intervene by targeting him with a huge bolt of lightning, causing him to grow two additional heads. King Ghidorah also has a new power: gravity beam. He lifts buildings into the sky and lets them drop, causing chaos and destruction across Japan. In terms of design, the special effects team continues to deliver megascale beasts, where every spike and scale looks real enough to touch. Godzilla is just as impressive. The only caveat being that he doesn't appear onscreen until the third act fight, which itself lasts only a few minutes out of the film's 135-minute runtime. Though the kaiju battle is exciting, likely due to its emulation of the director's cats fighting each other, a little more Godzilla screen time would have made the difference. New and returning characters Several familiar faces return from Godzilla Minus One, including the now-married couple of Koichi and Noriko Shikishima with their adopted daughter Akiko. Once again, they are forced to contend with the monsters in their world for the sake of their daughter. But they are not alone. Kenji Noda returns, now director of a monster-related disaster bureau, to come up with plans to fight Ghidorah with the help of newcomer Makoto Aoyama, a meteorologist who secretly shares the same pain as the ex-weapons engineer. Other recognizable players like the Shikishimas' motherly neighbor Sumiko and former battleship captain Tatsuo Hotta also return, older and wiser. Performances across the board carry the fear, awe and determination required to take on the kaijus; although, there are occasional moments of melodrama which feel over the top. The finale features one last conflict in the Shikishima family which seems unnecessary. While it features a heartbreaking callback to a previous goodbye, nothing would be lost in the story if the scene was cut. Responding to Oppenheimer It has been well established through various Godzilla projects that the monster is an allegory for the World War II atomic bomb attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki by the U.S. In an interview with Time Yamazaki recounted speaking to Christopher Nolan, director of that year's Best Picture Oppenheimer after Godzilla Minus One secured the Oscar for Best Visual Effects in 2024. "As part of our conversation I told him, 'One day I think I would like to make a response to your movie'… In my mind I was thinking I'd develop a film that looks directly at Hiroshima. But then I began thinking, 'Wait - Godzilla is itself a metaphor for nuclear war. Maybe I can combine the two and make a Godzilla movie that is also an answer to Oppenheimer," he said. Indeed, the film holds back zero punches as it tackles the aftermath of the atomic bomb on the Japanese people. The horrors of the bombs are displayed in all their gore and misery from those in the direct vicinity to those in the radiation zones who suffered slowly. Biologist Kanji Murakami, a survivor of Hiroshima, the first Godzilla attack and the first Ghidorah attack, has a vivid dream sequence that shows the extent of the suffering felt by the Japanese due to American actions in the wake of the bombing. Later in the film, U.S. officers are portrayed as one-dimensional, scheming individuals, while their soldiers are equal parts dumb and mean. A group of U.S. army men are tasked with stealing papers from Murakami relating to Godzilla's capabilities, with one chewing straw obnoxiously while their leader speaks in a Midwestern drawl. Ultimately, they are unsuccessful. It's a bold direction that is unusual to see on a U.S. theater screen, and one that resonates with the audience. While Oppenheimer may have shown us the guilt of Prometheus, it is important to reckon with the anguish and anger on the other side of the coin, something that Hollywood tends to keep muted. Closing thoughts Once again, Yamazaki has delivered a powerful and exciting Godzilla film that will resonate with both fans and non-fans alike. Though the eponymous star takes his time to make an entrance, King Ghidorah is a compelling and menacing force for the protagonists to contend with in the meantime. All the while, the unflinching treatment of the horrors of World War II from the Japanese perspective remains beneath the fantasy, serving as a thought-provoking and powerful reminder of Godzilla's true beginnings. So whether you're invested in the aftermath of atomic warfare, giant hyperrealistic monsters fighting each other or even just a classic underdog story of flawed heroes fighting for the ones they love, this story is for you.
